title: What metrics would you monitor for an EC2 instance / a Kubernetes cluster / a JVM app, and how do you achieve a high-availability SLA with monitoring + alerting?
shortTitle: What metrics to monitor for an EC2 instance, a Kubernetes cluster, and a JVM app, and how to achieve a high-availability SLA with monitoring and alerting

s1_definition.profdef: For an EC2 instance you monitor host-level resources — CPU utilization, memory, disk usage and disk I/O, network throughput, and status checks. For a Kubernetes cluster you monitor node health and capacity, pod status and restart counts, CPU and memory requests versus limits versus actual usage, pending pods, and control-plane health. For a JVM application you monitor heap and non-heap memory, garbage-collection frequency and pause time, thread counts, and application-level request rate, error rate, and latency. A high-availability SLA is achieved by combining redundancy (multiple instances across availability zones), automated health checks and failover, and monitoring with alerting on the user-facing golden signals so problems are caught and remediated before the SLA is breached.
s1_definition.analogy: Running the National Bank of India's systems is like running the building, the departments, and the individual clerks. The EC2 instance is the building — you watch its electricity, water, floor space, and whether the lights are on. The Kubernetes cluster is all the departments — you watch which departments are open, how many clerks each has, whether any department is overcrowded, and whether anyone is waiting outside with nowhere to sit. The JVM app is an individual clerk — you watch whether their desk is full of paper (heap), how often they stop work to tidy up (garbage collection), and how fast they serve Rajesh and Priya. High availability means you never rely on one clerk, one department, or one building — you have backups in different locations, and alarms that ring the moment any level starts to struggle, so you fix it before customers notice.
s1_definition.oneliner: Watch host resources on EC2, pod and node health on Kubernetes, heap and GC and latency on the JVM, and reach HA by combining multi-AZ redundancy with health-check failover and alerting on user-facing golden signals.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** For an EC2 instance you monitor host-level resources — CPU utilization, memory, disk usage and disk I/O, network throughput, and status checks. For a Kubernetes cluster you monitor node health and capacity, pod status and restart counts, CPU and memory requests versus limits versus actual usage, pending pods, and control-plane health. For a JVM application you monitor heap and non-heap memory, garbage-collection frequency and pause time, thread counts, and application-level request rate, error rate, and latency. A high-availability SLA is achieved by combining redundancy (multiple instances across availability zones), automated health checks and failover, and monitoring with alerting on the user-facing golden signals so problems are caught and remediated before the SLA is breached.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Running the National Bank of India's systems is like running the building, the departments, and the individual clerks. The EC2 instance is the building — you watch its electricity, water, floor space, and whether the lights are on. The Kubernetes cluster is all the departments — you watch which departments are open, how many clerks each has, whether any department is overcrowded, and whether anyone is waiting outside with nowhere to sit. The JVM app is an individual clerk — you watch whether their desk is full of paper (heap), how often they stop work to tidy up (garbage collection), and how fast they serve Rajesh and Priya. High availability means you never rely on one clerk, one department, or one building — you have backups in different locations, and alarms that ring the moment any level starts to struggle, so you fix it before customers notice.

**One line to remember:** Watch host resources on EC2, pod and node health on Kubernetes, heap and GC and latency on the JVM, and reach HA by combining multi-AZ redundancy with health-check failover and alerting on user-facing golden signals.

sections.s2_technical:
For an EC2 instance, the host-level metrics matter first. CPU utilization tells you if the box is saturated. Memory usage — which EC2 does not report by default, so you install the CloudWatch agent or a node exporter — tells you if you are about to swap or be out-of-memory killed. Disk usage matters because a full disk crashes applications and stops logging, and disk I/O (IOPS, throughput, queue depth) matters for database-like workloads. Network in and out shows throughput and helps spot saturation. EC2 status checks (system status and instance status) tell you if the underlying hardware or the instance itself is unhealthy, which drives automatic recovery.

For a Kubernetes cluster, you monitor at several layers. At the node layer you watch node readiness, allocatable versus used CPU and memory, and disk pressure. At the workload layer you watch pod phase (running, pending, failed), container restart counts (a climbing restart count signals crash loops), and whether pods are being OOM-killed or CPU-throttled because they hit their limits. A critical signal is pending pods, which means the scheduler cannot place them — usually insufficient capacity. You watch requests versus limits versus actual usage to right-size, and you watch control-plane health (API server latency, etcd health). The standard tools are kube-state-metrics for object state, node exporter and cAdvisor for resource usage, all scraped by Prometheus.

For a JVM application, the memory and garbage collector dominate. You watch heap used versus max, and especially the trend after each garbage collection — if used heap after a full GC keeps rising, you have a memory leak heading for an OutOfMemoryError. You watch GC frequency and pause times, because long or frequent pauses are stop-the-world events that spike latency for Rajesh's and Priya's transfers. You watch non-heap memory (metaspace), live thread count (a runaway thread count signals a leak or a stuck thread pool), and thread states (many BLOCKED threads signal lock contention). On top of the JVM internals you watch the application golden signals: request rate, error rate, and latency percentiles, exposed via Micrometer to Prometheus.

Achieving a high-availability SLA ties it all together. Redundancy is first: run multiple instances of each service spread across at least two or three availability zones, behind a load balancer, so the failure of one instance or one zone does not take down the service. Health checks and automated failover are second: the load balancer only routes to healthy instances, Kubernetes restarts failed pods and reschedules them to healthy nodes, and an auto-scaling group replaces unhealthy EC2 instances. Monitoring and alerting are third: you define SLIs that reflect the user experience (success rate, latency), set SLOs with an error budget, and alert on the golden signals with a sustained duration to avoid false positives. You test the whole thing with failure drills and you keep capacity headroom so a single instance failure does not immediately overload the survivors. A senior nuance: availability is not just uptime of a process but the fraction of requests served successfully within latency targets, so you measure it from the user's perspective, and you design so that no single component — not a database, not an availability zone, not a dependency — is a single point of failure.
sections.s3_banking:
The National Bank of India's transfer service must meet a 99.95 percent availability SLA. An on-call engineer needs a health monitor that watches all three layers and decides whether the service is healthy, degraded, or breaching its SLA.

Problem 1 — The EC2 host running a transfer pod is at ninety-five percent disk usage. If the disk fills, the app crashes and logging stops. The monitor must flag disk pressure before it becomes an outage.

Problem 2 — A transfer pod has restarted eight times in ten minutes, a crash loop, likely OOM-killed because its JVM heap is leaking. The monitor must detect the restart storm and the rising post-GC heap.

Problem 3 — Because the service runs three replicas across three availability zones, losing one pod still leaves two healthy, so the service stays available. The monitor must compute availability from healthy replicas and compare it to the SLA target.

Our runnable Java simulation models a `HealthMonitor` fed with an `Ec2Metrics`, a `K8sWorkload`, and a `JvmMetrics` snapshot, which evaluates each layer, computes an availability estimate from healthy replicas, and emits a verdict. Classes: `Ec2Metrics`, `K8sWorkload`, `JvmMetrics`, `HealthMonitor`, and a `HaMonitoringDemo` main.

##### 4c. Configuration File — the HA Kubernetes deployment

```yaml
# k8s/transfer-deployment.yaml — redundancy + health checks for HA
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: transfer-service
spec:
  replicas: 3                               # redundancy
  template:
    spec:
      # spread replicas across availability zones so one AZ loss != outage
      topologySpreadConstraints:
        - maxSkew: 1
          topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
          whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule
          labelSelector: { matchLabels: { app: transfer-service } }
      containers:
        - name: transfer
          image: nbi/transfer-service:1.4.2
          resources:
            requests: { cpu: "500m", memory: "512Mi" }
            limits:   { cpu: "1",    memory: "1Gi" }     # OOM-kill guard
          readinessProbe:                     # LB only routes to READY pods
            httpGet: { path: /actuator/health/readiness, port: 8080 }
            periodSeconds: 5
          livenessProbe:                       # restart a hung pod
            httpGet: { path: /actuator/health/liveness, port: 8080 }
            periodSeconds: 10
```

sections.s5_journey:
Input: a single health snapshot of the transfer service — an EC2 host at ninety-five percent disk, a Kubernetes deployment with two of three replicas ready and eight restarts in ten minutes, and a JVM with eighty-eight percent post-GC heap and 1400 milliseconds of GC pause per minute. The SLA target is 99.95 percent.

Step 1: The monitor evaluates the EC2 host. CPU and memory are fine, but disk is at ninety-five percent, which it flags as severe because a full disk would crash the app and stop logging. The status check is OK, so the hardware is healthy.

Step 2: The monitor evaluates the Kubernetes workload. Eight restarts in ten minutes is a crash loop, flagged severe and attributed to a likely OOM-kill. There are no pending pods, so cluster capacity is sufficient.

Step 3: The monitor evaluates the JVM. The post-GC heap at eighty-eight percent is flagged severe as a memory leak heading for an OutOfMemoryError, which explains the crash loop. The GC pause of 1400 milliseconds per minute is flagged as a latency risk for transfers.

Step 4: The monitor computes availability from healthy replicas. Two of three replicas are ready, and because the service only needs two to serve traffic, it is still available. The verdict is DEGRADED rather than a breach — the service is serving Rajesh's and Priya's transfers, but the engineer must remediate quickly.

Step 5: The remediation is to evict the pod off the full-disk node, roll the leaking pod so a fresh one starts, and let auto-scaling replace the bad EC2 host. Redundancy across availability zones is what kept the SLA intact during the incident.

```
2026-10-30 02:12:40 [INFO   ] National Bank of India — HA health monitor (SLA target 99.95%)
2026-10-30 02:12:40 [SEVERE ] EC2: disk at 95.0% — risk of crash & log loss
2026-10-30 02:12:40 [SEVERE ] K8s: 8 restarts/10m — crash loop (likely OOM-kill)
2026-10-30 02:12:40 [SEVERE ] JVM: post-GC heap 88.0% — memory leak heading for OutOfMemoryError
2026-10-30 02:12:40 [WARNING] JVM: GC pauses 1400ms/min — latency spikes for transfers
2026-10-30 02:12:40 [WARNING] SLA: DEGRADED — 2/3 ready; still serving but remediate fast
2026-10-30 02:12:40 [INFO   ] Remediation: evict pod off the full-disk node, roll the leaking pod, auto-scaling replaces the bad EC2 host; SLA protected by redundancy.
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Health snapshot (every scrape)
    │
    ├── EC2 LAYER: cpu 72% / mem 68% / disk 95% / status OK
    │       └─► disk>90% → SEVERE (crash & log-loss risk)
    │
    ├── K8S LAYER: desired=3 ready=2 restarts=8/10m pending=0
    │       └─► restarts≥5 → SEVERE (crash loop / OOM-kill)
    │
    ├── JVM LAYER: post-GC heap 88% / gc 1400ms/min / threads 240
    │       └─► heap>85% → SEVERE (leak → OOM)   gc>1s → WARN (latency)
    │
    ▼
  availability = ready/desired = 2/3; serving if ready≥2
    ├─ ready≥2 & ≥SLA → HEALTHY
    ├─ ready≥2        → DEGRADED (serve + remediate)   ← this run
    └─ ready<2        → BREACH RISK (failover/scale now)
    │
    ▼
  Remediation: evict off full disk, roll leak, ASG replaces host
  (redundancy across AZs kept the 99.95% SLA intact)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
For an EC2 instance I monitor the host resources: CPU utilization, memory usage — which I have to add with the CloudWatch agent or a node exporter because EC2 does not report it by default — disk usage and disk I/O, network throughput, and the system and instance status checks that drive automatic recovery. For a Kubernetes cluster I monitor at several layers: node readiness and allocatable capacity, pod phase, container restart counts which reveal crash loops, pods being OOM-killed or CPU-throttled against their limits, and pending pods which mean the scheduler cannot find capacity, using kube-state-metrics and cAdvisor scraped by Prometheus. For a JVM application I watch heap used versus max and especially the post-garbage-collection trend, because a rising floor means a leak heading for an OutOfMemoryError, plus garbage-collection frequency and pause times which directly spike request latency, thread counts, and the application golden signals of request rate, error rate, and latency exposed through Micrometer.

Achieving a high-availability SLA ties all of this together through three things. First is redundancy: I run multiple replicas of each service spread across at least two or three availability zones behind a load balancer, so losing one instance or one whole zone does not take the service down. Second is automated health checks and failover: the load balancer only routes to healthy instances, Kubernetes readiness and liveness probes restart hung pods and reschedule failed ones, and an auto-scaling group replaces unhealthy EC2 hosts automatically. Third is monitoring and alerting on the user-facing golden signals with a sustained duration so a blip never pages, measuring availability as the fraction of requests served successfully within latency targets rather than mere process uptime.

In my project at the National Bank of India, the transfer service had a 99.95 percent availability SLA and ran three replicas across three availability zones. During one incident a host hit ninety-five percent disk, a pod entered a crash loop from a JVM heap leak that was OOM-killing it, and the post-GC heap sat at eighty-eight percent. Because two of the three replicas stayed healthy across their zones, the service kept serving transfers between Rajesh's SAV2001 and Priya's CUR3001 — the verdict was degraded, not a breach. We evicted the pod off the full-disk node, rolled the leaking pod, and auto-scaling replaced the bad host, all while redundancy protected the SLA. The principle I always state is that high availability comes from designing so no single component is a point of failure, and from alerting on what the user actually experiences so you remediate before the error budget is spent.
